MA-onboarding-redesign · Gate 1, round 2

Onboarding Redesign — Three Visual Directions

Round 1 (mockup.html) was rejected on visual treatment only — the structure it locked stays: screen order, content order, the five-choice account-type matrix, the 32-colour sheet, the zero-shift geometry contract. Every frame below shares the exact same header (56px), 4-segment progress rail, and 52px footer CTA track as round 1 — that's the proof the geometry didn't move. What changes column to column is fill, gradient, glow, type scale, and motion.

This page shows the populated/default state only, on three representative screens (Welcome, First Account, Ready). Loading, error, and empty states keep round 1's exact geometry — recolouring or filling an already-reserved slot, never inserting one — so restyling them once a direction is picked is a skin change, not a re-spec.

What was dated, in order of how much it hurt

  1. Uppercase micro-labels on every field — fixed identically in all three columns below (sentence case, tight to the field). This one isn't a "direction," it's just correct.
  2. No material depth anywhere — every surface the same flat fill at the same radius.
  3. The welcome hero was a placeholder — a flat box with a small outline glyph.
  4. Timid type hierarchy — nothing on the page was allowed to be big.
  5. The account-type tiles were five identical grey boxes for the most important choice on N2.
  6. Uniform full-width stacking — no composition, no grouping, no asymmetry.
  7. The CTA was a flat gold slab — no depth, no edge, no light.
  8. The currency toggle was a plain segmented control on the app's first-impression screen.
Hard constraints respected in all three: no expo-blur, no glassmorphism (Android/web paint it as flat opaque colour — HeroUI's own docs say so), no new dependencies, no native code, every HeroUI primitive kept. Contrast checked: gold-on-background and gold-on-surface both clear 7:1 (AA needs 4.5:1); every tap target — currency tabs, type-grid cells, the CTA — holds at 44pt or above even where the direction goes typographic. One open risk is called out plainly in Direction C's rationale rather than drawn as if it were free.
A · Material & Depth

Vault

HeroShell's own formula, extended

Commits to reusing the app's one proven premium surface — hero_shell.tsx's diagonal gradient, 3% grid texture, corner glow, hairline border — on the moments that matter: the welcome hero, the selected type tile, the Ready summary card, the CTA. Nothing invented; this is what the dashboard already ships on Android with zero new dependencies.

Costs more render nodes per screen — a gradient plus an SVG texture per elevated element instead of one flat fill — and more surface area where a gradient has to hold its exact geometry under the zero-shift contract.

Risky at: HeroShell reads as premium on the dashboard because it appears exactly once, as a hero. Apply it to six things on one screen and the specialness dilutes — so only the selected tile, the hero, the summary card, and the CTA get it here. Everything else stays deliberately flat.

B · Typography & Composition

Broadsheet

Scale and asymmetry, not chrome

Commits to letting scale do what material does in the other two columns — oversized Sora numerals, a left-aligned ragged composition, a thin gold column rule, a ghost numeral as pure-typographic decoration instead of an illustration. No new gradients, no new render layers — the cheapest of the three to build and the lightest on a mid-range Android GPU.

Costs material richness entirely. N1 and N4 go close to flat next to columns A and C — the bet is that confidence of scale reads as premium on its own.

Risky at: oversized type has the least room to survive real content. A longer account name, a longer error string, or a device at 130% text scale is where this breaks first — needs the tightest copy discipline of the three and real dynamic-type testing before it ships.

C · Light & Motion

Aurora

Colour and glow as the premium signal

Commits to a soft two-hue ambient wash (gold + Nile teal), a glowing halo the instant a user picks something, a shimmer sweep on the CTA — all genuine screen-native techniques (react-native-svg radial gradients, not blur). The most viscerally "fancy" of the three and the one most likely to read as new.

Costs the most animation — a continuously looping shimmer and a breathing glow are a real battery and Android-GPU cost paid on every onboarding screen, not once.

Risky at: N2 is a dense form. Ambient light that reads as premium on the calm welcome and ready screens fights legibility once 5 fields are on screen, so this direction has to dial itself back exactly where the user is looking hardest. Flagging plainly, not drawing around it: the gold-to-teal gradient headline text below needs react-native-svg's Text with a gradient fill — possible with what's installed, but nothing in this codebase does it today. Treat it as unverified until tariq spikes it; the cheap fallback is flat gold text, which is what I'd actually ship.

Recommendation

Ship A — Vault.

It's the only one of the three that isn't actually a new idea for this app. hero_shell.tsx already proved gradient + grid texture + corner glow + hairline border reads as premium on Android — the platform onboarding actually has to work well on — with zero new dependencies. Extending a pattern that's already shipped and already battle-tested beats importing a new visual language for four screens a user sees exactly once. It also lands the most direct hits on the specific things called dated: no material depth, the placeholder hero, the grey account-type tiles, the flat CTA — all four get fixed by the same one formula, applied selectively rather than everywhere.

Two things I'd still take from the other columns

  • B's field-label fix — sentence case, tight tracking, close to the field. This was diagnosis item #1, the single most dating thing on the page, and it isn't really a "direction" — it's just correct. Apply it regardless of which column ships.
  • B's bigger N4 hero number. 31px undersells the one number onboarding exists to produce. Taking it toward the 40px scale MoneyApp already uses for amount entry costs nothing structurally and is the cheapest high-impact fix on the table.

What I'd leave out of C

The continuously looping shimmer and the breathing glow. Reserve one shimmer sweep, once, non-looping, for the N4 CTA only — onboarding's one true arrival moment — and skip it everywhere else. A continuous animation running on four screens a user passes through a single time is a battery cost paid by everyone for a delight almost no one stays long enough to notice.

What's left for you to decide

  • Whether to ship pure A, or A with the two B elements folded in (my actual recommendation).
  • If any part of C survives — even just the N4 CTA shimmer — tariq should spike SvgText gradient fill on a real Android device before it's designed in for real; the fallback (flat gold text) costs nothing and I'd be equally happy shipping it.
  • Whether a single non-looping arrival animation on N4 is worth the implementation time at all, or whether the static gold CTA (what A already has) is enough.
